sections.page: Verify webhook signatures in Node, PHP, Python, Java and Go
sections.markdown: Every delivery is an HTTPS `POST` with a JSON body and a `X-Strait-Signature` header. Anyone can send your endpoint a POST, so check the signature before you trust the body. The verifiers on this page use only each language's standard library, and every one of them is tested in our build against signatures made by our server's own signing code. For events, retries and the delivery log, see [Webhooks](https://straitlink.in/docs/webhooks/).

sections.page: Verify webhook signatures in Node, PHP, Python, Java and Go
sections.section: 1. Store the signing secret on your server
sections.markdown:
Copy the **signing secret** when you create the webhook in **Dashboard → Settings → Webhooks**. It's shown once. Put it in your server's environment as `WEBHOOK_SECRET`, next to your secret API key, and never in an app or a website.

**You should see:** `WEBHOOK_SECRET` set in the environment your webhook handler runs in (for example `echo ${WEBHOOK_SECRET:0:5}` prints its first characters).

sections.page: Verify webhook signatures in Node, PHP, Python, Java and Go
sections.markdown:
The header looks like this:

```txt
X-Strait-Signature: t=1800000000,v1=adf19a16865985b0891b0e7e4f6770e17d6bdd6462d897848f5adb661c4381bb
```

- `t` is the Unix time in seconds when we signed this attempt.
- `v1` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the string `<t>.<raw body>`: the value of `t`, a full stop, then the exact bytes of the request body, keyed with your signing secret.

So your check is: split the header on `,` and each part on the first `=`, refuse a `t` more than 300 seconds from your clock (either way), compute the HMAC yourself and compare it with `v1` in constant time. Every retry is signed again with a fresh `t`.

Use this vector to test your code before any real delivery:

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Secret | `whsec` |
| Raw body | `{"a":1}` |
| `t` | `1800000000` |
| Expected header | `t=1800000000,v1=adf19a16865985b0891b0e7e4f6770e17d6bdd6462d897848f5adb661c4381bb` |

**You should see:** the same `v1` from your language's HMAC function, for example `printf '%s' '1800000000.{"a":1}' | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac whsec` prints `adf19a16…381bb`.

sections.page: Verify webhook signatures in Node, PHP, Python, Java and Go
sections.markdown:
Delivery is at least once: a retry carries the same `X-Strait-Delivery` id (also `id` in the body) and a new signature. Store the ids you've handled, for example in a table with a unique key or Redis with `SET NX` and a 7-day expiry, and return `2xx` for a repeat without doing the work again.

**You should see:** when you send your endpoint the same logged body and headers twice within 5 minutes, the event is handled once and both requests get `2xx`.

sections.page: Verify webhook signatures in Node, PHP, Python, Java and Go
sections.markdown:
- **Every signature fails, even the test event.** The body was parsed before you hashed it (`express.json()`, Spring with a `String` or object, Laravel `$request->all()`). Hash the raw bytes, as in step 4. Also check the secret has no stray quotes or newline from your `.env` file.
- **Signatures pass locally but fail in production.** The server clock is off by more than 5 minutes. Turn on NTP time sync.
- **A proxy or gateway rejects or rewrites the request.** Some API gateways re-encode JSON or strip unknown headers. Pass `X-Strait-Signature` through and leave the body untouched.

sections.markdown: WhatsApp only lets a business start a chat with a **template**: "Template messages are the only type of message that can be sent to WhatsApp users outside of a customer service window", and only templates with `APPROVED` status can be sent ([Meta: Template fundamentals](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/templates/overview)). This recipe puts a Strait link in the template's URL button, so one approved template can carry a different link for each campaign. Meta's API details below are quoted from Meta's docs as of October 2026; check the linked pages before you go live.

sections.page: Send campaign links via WhatsApp Business API templates
sections.markdown:
Create a link whose destination carries the campaign's UTM tags. The tags tell Analytics the channel and campaign, and `title`, `description` and `imageUrl` set the preview when the link is shared in a chat:

```bash
curl https://strait.link/v1/links \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SECRET_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "slug": "diwali",
    "longUrl": "https://shop.example.com/sale/diwali?utm_source=whatsapp&utm_campaign=diwali-2026",
    "title": "Diwali sale",
    "description": "Up to 40% off lights and gifts",
    "imageUrl": "https://shop.example.com/img/diwali.jpg"
  }'
```

Then check what a tap from WhatsApp's browser does, without counting a tap:

```bash
curl "https://strait.link/v1/simulate?url=https%3A%2F%2Fhilltop.strait.link%2Fdiwali&ua=whatsapp-android" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SECRET_KEY"
```

**You should see:** `"shortUrl": "https://hilltop.strait.link/diwali"` from the first call, and `"inAppBrowser": "whatsapp"` with your link's `slug` from the second.

Open **Dashboard → Analytics** and pick `diwali-2026` in the **Campaign** filter. Taps count under the WhatsApp channel because of the `utm_source` on the destination, and taps inside WhatsApp's own browser are labelled WhatsApp anyway. On Android, someone without the app goes through Google Play and lands on the sale screen on the first launch (iPhone install matching is in public beta). sections.section: The link opens the browser instead of the app
sections.markdown:
This almost always means the phone couldn't verify that your app may open links on your domain.

Start with the free [App Links checker](https://straitlink.in/tools/app-links-checker/): it fetches both files from your domain and explains what's wrong with them (missing file, redirect, wrong content type, malformed fingerprint or app ID).

1. **Check the file.** `curl https://hilltop.strait.link/.well-known/assetlinks.json` should list your package name and fingerprints. A `404` means the Android fields in Settings are empty.
2. **Check the SHA-256.** The fingerprint must match the certificate of the build on the phone:
   - Debug builds: your debug keystore.
   - Release builds you install yourself: your upload key.
   - Builds from Google Play: the **App signing key** in Play Console → App integrity. This is Google's key, not yours.
3. **Check the intent filter**: `android:autoVerify="true"`, `https` scheme, and `android:host="hilltop.strait.link"` exactly.
4. **Re-verify.** Android checks at install time. Reinstall the app, then run `adb shell pm get-app-links com.yourco.app`. You want `verified`.
5. **Tap, don't type.** Pasting a link into the address bar never opens an app. Test from Messages, WhatsApp or Gmail.

On iPhone (beta): check `apple-app-site-association` lists `<Team ID>.<bundle ID>`, and the app has `applinks:hilltop.strait.link` in Associated Domains. iOS caches the file through Apple's CDN, so changes can take a while to show.

When the person taps a link on a page in Samsung Internet, it handles our hand-off like Chrome: if the app is installed it opens; if not, it goes to Google Play. When an unverified link is handed to Samsung Internet from another app (an SMS or email app), there's no tap inside the browser, and in our real-phone test (Samsung Internet 30, 3 October 2026) it went to Google Play even though the app was installed. Verified App Links avoid this, because Android opens the app before any browser runs ([details](https://straitlink.in/blog/samsung-internet-intent-link-opens-play-store/)). If Samsung Internet keeps opening links in the browser, check **Settings → Useful features → Open links in other apps** is on.

sections.section: Firefox and Edge ask before opening the app
sections.markdown: Firefox ("Open this link in …?") and Edge ("wants to open an external app") show a confirmation before handing a link to an app. That's the browser's choice and can't be skipped. Once the person confirms, the app opens on the right screen and the tap is counted once.

In-app browsers often don't open apps or app stores from a link on their own, so a deep link may not work inside them. We detect them and show a page made for them: on Android an **Open in app** button, and everywhere steps to open the link in the real browser, where it works normally. To skip that step, share links where possible in places that hand them to the phone's browser or app, for example Messages.

sections.section: The deferred link didn't open the right screen after install
sections.markdown:
- **Android**: the app must be installed **from Google Play** (internal testing is fine). Sideloaded builds have no install referrer. In Settings, set "When someone without the app taps a link" to **Always Google Play** while your app isn't public, otherwise we send people to your website to avoid Play's "Item not found" page.
- **iPhone (beta)**: the person must tap **Get the app** on our page in Safari, and open the app within an hour, on the same network. A different network (Wi-Fi to cellular) will usually prevent a match.
- **Both**: the deferred check runs once per install. Uninstall and reinstall to test again.

sections.section: The app opened but `matched` is false
sections.markdown:
Check `reason` on the link event:

| Reason | What it means |
|---|---|
| `not_found` | No such link in this workspace (check the publishable key and the slug) |
| `expired` | The link's expiry has passed |
| `password_protected` | Password links can't be opened directly in the app |
| `no_match` | Deferred: no recent matching tap |
| `network` | The phone couldn't reach us. The open is saved and reported later |
| `invalid_url` | The URL couldn't be parsed |
Email [support@straitlink.in](mailto:support@straitlink.in) with the link, the phone model, the browser or app you tapped it in, and what happened.

sections.page: Test mode for deferred deep links (coming soon)
sections.markdown: Seeing a deferred deep link work today takes a build installed from Google Play (the link travels in the Play Install Referrer) or, on iPhone (beta), a device match. Both are slow to set up for a first check. Test mode is a shortcut for one question only: *is my app wired up so that the first open lands on the link's screen?*

sections.page: Test mode for deferred deep links (coming soon)
sections.markdown:
1. In **Dashboard → Get started**, a writer turns on test mode. That opens a 15-minute window for the workspace.
2. On your phone, tap any of your links. WhatsApp works.
3. Install and open your **debug** build with test mode on in the SDK.
4. The first device that checks in during the window becomes the workspace's test device. It gets your most recent tap since the window opened, once, and the SDK hands it to your app exactly like a real deferred link: `kind: 'deferred'` in the same `onLink` callback.

The dashboard shows the result and, when nothing matched, why: no window open, a different device already used it, or no tap since you turned it on (tap your link and reopen the app).

sections.page: Test mode for deferred deep links (coming soon)
sections.markdown:
- **Run in release builds.** The SDK sends the test request only from debug builds; your production app never does.
- **Change your numbers.** A test match records no install and no app open, and the tap isn't marked as matched. Analytics and billing are unchanged.
- **Touch real matching.** Real users are matched exactly as they are today, with or without test mode.
- **Use a hardware or advertising ID.** The test device is a random id the SDK creates once in the debug build.
